title: Predict the output: a loop that adds i to a List<Short> and then removes the last element whenever size > 1: what prints and why?
shortTitle: Predict output: loop adding to List<Short> with removal: autoboxing trap
keyPoints: List.remove(int) removes by INDEX, List.remove(Object) removes by VALUE
When the argument is a primitive int or short widened to int, Java calls remove(int index), not remove(Object)
To remove by value, explicitly box the argument: list.remove(Short.valueOf(i)) or list.remove((Integer) i)
This is an autoboxing overload resolution trap -- one of the most common Java interview puzzles
removeIf(predicate) is the safest way to remove by value because it avoids the overload ambiguity
The issue applies to List<Integer>, List<Short>, and List<Long> -- any boxed numeric wrapper

s1_definition.oneliner: List.remove(int) removes by index, List.remove(Object) removes by value. When the argument is a primitive int, Java picks the index overload, causing unexpected behavior with numeric wrapper lists.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **remove(int index)** removes the element at the specified position in the list.
- **remove(Object o)** removes the first occurrence of the specified element by value.
- When the argument is a primitive `int` or `short` (widened to `int`), Java resolves to `remove(int index)` because an exact `int` overload exists.
- Autoboxing to `Short`/`Integer` does NOT happen during overload resolution when an `int` overload exists.
- To force value removal, explicitly box: `list.remove(Short.valueOf(i))` or cast: `list.remove((Short) (short) i)`.
- The safest alternative is `removeIf(x -> x == target)` which has no overload ambiguity.
s1_definition.analogy: You add cheque numbers 1, 2, 3 to a box. You say "remove 1". Did you mean remove cheque number 1 (by value) or remove the cheque at position 1 (by index)? Java picks "by index" when the argument is int, and "by value" when it is a Short object. This ambiguity causes the surprise.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  List<Integer> nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]

  nums.remove(1)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Argument: int 1                     │
  │ Match: remove(int index)            │
  │ Action: remove element at index 1   │
  │ Removed: 20                         │
  │ Result: [10, 30, 40]                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

  nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(30))
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Argument: Integer 30                │
  │ Match: remove(Object o)             │
  │ Action: remove first occurrence of 30│
  │ Removed: 30                         │
  │ Result: [10, 40]                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The autoboxing trap occurs because `List` has two `remove` overloads: `remove(int index)` for position-based removal and `remove(Object)` for value-based removal. When the argument is a primitive `int` or `short` (widened to `int`), Java calls the index overload because overload resolution prefers widening over boxing.

To remove by value, explicitly box the argument: `list.remove(Short.valueOf(i))` or use `removeIf(x -> x == target)` which has no overload ambiguity. The `removeIf` approach is the safest and most readable.

At National Bank of India, a list of short settlement codes is pruned in a loop. Calling `remove(code)` where `code` is a primitive `short` (widened to `int`) silently deletes the wrong element and corrupts the batch. Using `removeIf` prevents this bug.

Remember one sentence: remove(int) is by index, remove(Object) is by value, and Java picks by-index when the argument is a primitive int.
